lead: A GIS — a Geographic Information System — is an organised set of five parts: hardware, software, data, people and methods. It captures, stores, manages, analyses and displays data that carries a location, so questions of the form 'where is what, and what lies near it' get an answer. The idea exists because a printed map can only show, while a decision needs two or more layers compared. It is used wherever place decides the answer: a metro alignment, a rural school site, a drought relief list, a water network. This chapter defines the system and separates it from software that merely draws maps.
prereq: You need: map scale and topographic sheets from Unit 1, and the idea of a remote sensing image from Unit 6.

blocks.text: A GIS is a system that captures, stores, manages, analyses and displays spatially referenced data — data tied to a place on the earth — so that people can answer a question and take a decision. Each record carries a position: coordinates, or a named area such as a ward or a survey number.
The system has five parts. Drop one and it stops being a GIS.

items: Hardware: computers, servers, phones, GNSS receivers, scanners and plotters.
Software: the program that holds layers and runs overlay, buffer and query.
Data: the layers — points, lines, areas, images — with their attributes. Usually the costliest part of a project.
People: the surveyor who captures, the analyst who queries, the engineer who decides.
Methods (procedures): the written rules — datum and projection, scale, checking, acceptable error.

blocks.text: Four functions run through these parts. Input turns a paper map, a total station file, a GNSS track or a satellite image into a layer. Storage and management keep the layers in a database along with topology — the recorded rules that say which line meets which, and which area lies inside which. Manipulation and analysis combine layers by buffer, overlay and query (the operations are worked out in 7.6). Output gives the answer as a map, a table or a report.

Some syllabi write Geographical Information System, others Geospatial Information System. The meaning is the same. In an exam, defend the last word, System. The data is geospatial, and the computer is only a tool; the system includes people and written methods, which is why a mapping program alone is not a GIS.

sections.h3: GIS is not a map drawer

blocks.text: Four familiar tools look like a GIS at a glance. Each one stops before the analysis.

head: Tool
What it does
Where it stops
rows: geometry only; no attribute table joined to place, no overlay
a name and a number, no position; cannot ask 'what is near'
a data source, one input among many
displays a map, finds a route
shows ready layers; the user cannot add a layer and overlay it

blocks.text: A GIS differs from all four in one habit: it answers by combining layers through location. 'Which streets lie within 200 m of this point and carry no water main' is a GIS question. A phone map shows the streets; it does not know your water mains.
Exam test: if the sentence contains only display, it is digital mapping. If it has one layer, another layer and a place-based condition, it is GIS.

sections.h3: History, Indian use, and the questions it answers

blocks.text: The first computer-based GIS was built in the 1960s for the Canada Land Inventory under Roger Tomlinson, to hold land capability, land use and ownership over large areas and to answer where land suited what. In the same decade a graphics laboratory at Harvard produced early computer mapping programs. These ran on mainframes, and one overlay could take hours.

Through the 1970s and 1980s GIS moved to minicomputers and then to desktop personal computers. Vector storage with topology became standard and commercial packages appeared. The 1990s made GNSS a routine input. After 2000 it moved to the web, then to the cloud, so a phone can send a position and receive an answer from a server.

In India, ISRO and NRSC run Bhuvan, a national geoportal that serves satellite imagery and thematic layers, and Survey of India supplies digital topographic data. State remote sensing centres apply the same layers to district planning. Everyday use is quieter: a cab app matching the nearest driver, a delivery route, a crop-insurance claim checked against a field boundary.

items: Drought management: rainfall, soil, crop and groundwater layers together mark the villages needing relief first.
Rural school planning: child population, walking distance and existing buildings overlay to fix a new site.
Building attributes: roof footprints and heights read from imagery into a layer with attributes.
Zonal planning: remote sensing land-use classes combined with administrative boundaries to fix zones.
Civil engineering: alignments, cut and fill, utility clashes and site progress tracked as layers.

examples.question: A city engineer must list every street within 200 m of a proposed metro station that has no water main. Three layers exist, all in metres on the same projection: street centre lines, water mains of 600 mm diameter, and the station point. Work the steps and state the area searched.
steps: Input and check: the three layers must share datum, projection and units (see 7.5). Layers that do not line up give a wrong answer silently.
Buffer the station point at radius R = 200 m. Area of the circle = πR² = π × 200² = 125 663.71 m², about 12.57 hectares.
Clip the street layer to that buffer. Only street segments inside the circle remain, and each kept segment is treated as a complete street, not a trimmed piece.

Buffer every water main by half its width: a 600 mm main gives 0.600 ÷ 2 = 0.300 m. Find the kept street segments that touch these buffered mains and remove those whole segments, rather than shaving a narrow band along them.
The segments left over are complete streets with no main. Plot them on the ward map and tabulate their names — this is the output function.
The engineer chooses the new pipe route — this is the people component deciding.
examples.answer: The search covers 125 663.71 m² (about 12.57 ha) around the station, mains are buffered by 0.300 m, and the street segments that do not touch a buffered main form the answer list.
examples.check:
import math
r = 200.0
area = math.pi * r**2
print(round(area, 2))
print(0.600 / 2)

traps: Writing 'GIS = Google Maps', 'GIS = a satellite image' or 'GIS = mapping software'. The examiner wants a system of five components and four functions, with analysis named as the difference.
Listing hardware and software only. People and methods are components too, and data is normally the largest cost.
Calling remote sensing a part of GIS, or GIS a part of remote sensing. Remote sensing is a data source; GIS is the system that analyses it.
Naming GPS or GNSS as a component. It is an input device and a source of positions, not one of the five parts.
History answers that give a date with no name, or a name with no work. Roger Tomlinson and the Canada Land Inventory is the pair expected.

quiz.q: Name the five components of a GIS.
State the four functions of a GIS in order.
quiz.a: Data input; storage and management; manipulation and analysis; output.

quiz.q: Why is a plain database not a GIS?
quiz.a: It stores records without position, so 'what is near what' cannot be asked. A GIS joins attributes to place and combines layers by location.

quiz.q: A satellite image is called a data source for GIS, not a GIS. Explain.
quiz.a: The image supplies one layer of measurements or classes. A GIS stores it with other layers, analyses the combination and produces a decision output.

quiz.q: A station point is buffered at 150 m. Find the buffer area in m² and in hectares.
A team owns satellite images, a mapping program and a plotter and claims it has a GIS. What is missing and which function fails?
quiz.a: Missing a database of layers with attributes and topology, analysis tools, staff with defined roles (capture, analysis, decision) and written methods on datum, projection and accuracy. The analysis function fails: it can display but cannot buffer or overlay.

beyond: Not for the exam. Practice now splits into desktop GIS, web GIS and cloud GIS, with scripting replacing menu clicks wherever an analysis must be repeated. Open standards let layers move between agencies without conversion loss. Research runs on real-time sensor streams, 3D city models built from LiDAR, and machine learning on raster layers.
